seed_variation.verdict: Only one seed was run, so there is no seed variation to measure.
seed_variation.why: A hosted LLM cannot be seeded: our seeds only reach local random generators, and the provider's sampling (temperature etc.) is fixed for this model. So every run can give different text, and the spread across seeds measures the model's own run-to-run variation. Each seed repeats every API call. Each seed sets Python random, NumPy and torch. PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed to the FIRST seed for the whole run.

predictions.SY0103a: Laura, Laura, Tomasz, Priya, and Ben held a kick-off meeting for a new voice-controlled kitchen timer. Laura outlined the financial constraints, noting a target retail price of twenty-five euros, a maximum production cost of twelve fifty per unit, and a company profit goal of fifteen million. The team agreed that the device should operate on-device with a fixed vocabulary, a wake word to prevent false triggers, and a single physical backup button to stop the alarm. Tomasz raised concerns about power drain and component costs versus batteries, while Priya suggested the device should provide short voice confirmations and support multiple timers. Finally, Laura assigned action items to prepare for the functional design meeting in thirty minutes.
predictions.SY0103b: The team discussed the functional design for the voice-controlled kitchen timer while Tomasz was absent due to illness. They updated the timer concept from three named timers to two numbered timers, timer one and timer two, to avoid recognition and memory issues identified in user research. They also agreed on a core command list, a loud escalating alarm, positioning the device as a giftable kitchen gadget, and adopted Kiko as the working name subject to acoustic testing. Decisions on a small digital display and power source were parked until Tomasz provides his cost and hardware breakdown.
predictions.SY0103c: The team reviewed conceptual design options for their offline voice-controlled timer, keeping to the twenty-five euro selling price and twelve-fifty production limit. They agreed to use mains power via USB-C with an adapter in the box and include a small two-digit LED display, bringing the unit cost to eleven-thirty. Priya presented the command list, and the team confirmed Kiko as the wake word after discussing minor false triggers. Marketing research showed strong potential against smart speakers by emphasizing that the product requires no app, no Wi-Fi, and operates completely offline. Finally, they agreed on a round, wipeable plastic casing where the entire top functions as a rubber button with the display in the center.
predictions.SY0103d: The team reviewed the detailed design of the voice timer, covering the wake word test results, physical model, user interface, aesthetics, and cost evaluation. Supplier retraining resolved false triggers on the word cocoa, and Tomasz will test the wake word on the real development board once it arrives. The physical model features a palm-sized foam and rubber body with a full-top button, a central display window, and a low USB-C port, with rubber feet added for stability. The display will alternate between two running timers using a decimal point indicator, dropping the previous double-press idea. The button will stop ringing with a short press and cancel both timers when held for three seconds. The team selected two colourways (white with an orange top, and charcoal with a lime green top) using a white LED display, and Tomasz will request colour samples from the moulding supplier. The unit cost stands at eleven forty, leaving a small safety margin below the twelve fifty target, and final evaluation confirmed the product meets its original goals of being hands-free, loud, and competitively priced.
predictions.SY0110a: Priya opened the kickoff meeting for a reusable coffee cup project with a deposit system, joined by Tom as industrial designer and Jonas as user interface designer, while Marta was absent at a trade fair. The team reviewed project targets, including a one-euro deposit, a production cost under three euros, and fifty partner cafes in the first year. Initial design ideas were discussed, deciding that the cup must be dishwasher-safe and fit standard lids, while collapsible designs and an app for return tracking were left pending Marta's input. Priya assigned homework tasks for the next meeting.
predictions.SY0110b: The team met for their second functional design meeting to finalise cup materials, return processes, and functional requirements. After reviewing options, they selected polypropylene for its durability and cost, rejecting stainless steel, bamboo fibre, and silicone, and planned a commercial dishwasher test at Café Lindner instead of the office kitchen. For the return process, the team decided on simple counter returns at participating cafes without an app, using partner window badges for identification. They also confirmed a ninety-millimetre rim, stackable design, and space for cafe logos, while keeping the one-euro deposit constraint.
predictions.SY0110c: The team reviewed the dishwasher test results for the polypropylene cups and agreed to use in-mould labelling for the logo, a ribbed band for gripping, and a single three-hundred-millilitre size in slate grey. They also discussed counter return flows, agreeing on a refund or swap system, and reviewed the partner cafe badge design. Finally, they assigned tasks for the upcoming detailed design phase.
predictions.SY0110d: The team held their final detailed design meeting while Jonas was absent due to illness, starting with a review of action items and project updates. Industrial Designer reported a production cost of one euro fifty-four per cup for an initial order of ten thousand units in slate grey polypropylene, and Project Manager confirmed management agreed to cover unreturned cups funded by a five-euro monthly partner fee. Marketing Expert presented the one-page staff guide, which was approved with a request for lamination and an added note about cracked cups. Industrial Designer walked through the final cup specifications, including an embossed text on the base regarding the one-euro deposit, while rejecting a second color run. Finally, the team verified that the design meets dishwasher, lid, cost, and deposit requirements, and assigned final tasks before closing.
predictions.SY0202a: Project manager Marcus convened the kickoff meeting for a new self-checkout kiosk project aimed at public libraries. The team, including industrial designer Tomas, marketing expert Priya, and user interface designer Hannah, discussed the scope, agreeing that the kiosk will handle checkouts and renewals using barcodes or digital app codes, but leave returns to existing library drops. They reviewed budget and design constraints, noting a strict production cost limit under four thousand euros, and touched on optional features such as receipts, physical buttons, and accessibility. Finally, Marcus assigned initial tasks for the upcoming functional design meeting and agreed to circulate the project brief and notes.
predictions.SY0202b: The team met to discuss the functional design of the library kiosk, covering hardware components, accessibility requirements, and barcode versus RFID options. Tomas presented the hardware layout, cost estimates, and wood panelling design, while Priya shared user research indicating a need for speed, optional printed receipts for older borrowers, audio support for visually impaired users, and a physical help button. The group agreed on email as the default receipt method with a print option, incorporating audio mode, and adding a hardware help button. Priya took over checking RFID pricing using existing library supplier lists, and Tomas agreed to sketch the casing design with updated shelf heights for the next meeting.
predictions.SY0202c: The team held their third conceptual design meeting, reviewing RFID pricing, casing sketches, and the user interface flow. They decided to use both an RFID reader pad and a barcode scanner fallback, and selected a tilted desk casing made of oak veneer with aluminium corners. Hannah presented the updated interface flow, integrating stack scanning and renewal options, and it was agreed to keep the fifteen-inch screen size for now, pending a physical mock-up. Tomas agreed to build a foam board mock-up of the desk version and research text-to-speech engines with the embedded board, Hannah will finalize the screens and audio script, and Priya will prepare evaluation criteria.
predictions.SY0202d: The team met for their final detailed design review, with Hannah absent due to a conference. Tomas presented a foam-board mock-up, leading the group to compromise on a seventeen-inch screen to stay within height and budget limits. Tomas also recommended a licensed industrial board with a built-in text-to-speech engine to ensure better audio quality for users. Priya outlined her evaluation criteria, scoring the design highly across speed, accessibility, library look, ease of use, print options, and staff help. Finally, the team calculated the unit cost at three thousand four hundred and ten euros, leaving a healthy headroom, and reviewed action items before wrapping up.
predictions.SY0209a: Laura opened the kickoff meeting for the new educational tablet case project with team members Tomasz, Priya, and Ben, setting the target age group at four to eight years old and confirming the case is exclusively for the Learnly seven-inch tablet. The team discussed financial constraints, noting a twenty-five Euro selling price and a maximum production cost of twelve fifty, and brainstormed design requirements including drop protection, a handle, wipeable materials, and a raised lip to protect the screen. Finally, Laura assigned action items for research and design before wrapping up the session.
predictions.SY0209b: The team met for their second functional design meeting, noting that Tomasz was absent due to illness. They reviewed survey feedback highlighting durability and cleaning needs, and discussed drop test targets and materials, agreeing on a one point two metre drop target and EVA foam for the body. The discussion then covered functional features, deciding on a fixed handle, covered buttons for power and volume, open cut-outs for the charging port and camera, and a raised screen lip while dropping swappable covers and fold-out stands. Finally, they assigned action items for sketches, costings, survey updates, and price checks for the next meeting.
predictions.SY0209c: The team reviewed survey results showing drop protection and cleaning as top priorities, with teachers wanting a name tag feature and parents preferring bright but dirt-hiding colours. Ben presented a supplier quote of eight euro forty for the case, and Priya shared her handle and button cut-out sketches. The group agreed to include a shallow wedge back and a name tag window if its cost stays under one euro, and selected strong blue and lime green as the launch colours. Finally, Ben agreed to get a revised quote, Priya will update her sketches, and Tomasz will prepare design evaluation criteria based on the survey.
predictions.SY0209d: The team met for their final detailed design meeting, reviewing cost estimates, design sketches, and evaluation criteria. They agreed on a foam pocket with clear film for the name tag on the back of the case and decided against adding a shoulder strap for safety reasons. Tomasz presented evaluation scores based on a recent survey, which mostly resulted in ones and twos, indicating a positive overall design assessment.
predictions.SY0304a: Project Manager Hannah, Marketing Expert Priya, and User Interface Designer Tom held a kickoff meeting for a new university campus parking availability display project, joined in absentia by industrial designer Marcus. The team reviewed the brief from the estates office, noting a tight manufacturing budget of four pounds per unit and a deadline for the start of next term, while agreeing that target users include staff, students, and visitors. They discussed initial design concepts combining space numbers with color indicators, and touched upon sustainability and sensing options before assigning action items and scheduling the next meeting for the following week.
predictions.SY0304b: The team met for a functional design meeting to review project research and nail down specifications. Priya presented survey results showing strong demand for distant readability and color coding, while Marcus outlined sensing options and recommended barrier counters with nightly resets. Tom presented layout sketches, leading to the decision to use a sixty-centimetre LED sign featuring the car park name and specific color thresholds. The team agreed on mains power drawn from the barrier supply and finalized the per-sign budget at around four hundred pounds. Finally, the project manager assigned action items regarding site checks, layouts, additional visitor feedback, and estate queries.
predictions.SY0304c: The team reviewed the conceptual design for the car park sign project. The project manager reported that the central sign near the main gate lacks budget and will be deferred. The user interface designer presented the sixty-centimetre layout with navy trim, and after feedback from the open day, agreed to add a parking symbol and drop the flashing warning feature. The marketing expert shared open day findings showing visitors struggled with car park names. The project manager discussed mains connection issues from Marcus's update, noting that four car parks have a supply at the barrier while the underground library car park requires a new power supply and a wall bracket mounting. The team confirmed a navy powder-coated aluminium casing and noted the per-sign cost sits tight at three hundred and ninety pounds.
predictions.SY0304d: The team met for their final detailed design meeting for the car park sign project. They reviewed electrics and mounting, confirming that estates will fund the library sign's electrical supply while surface car parks will use galvanised steel posts and the library will use a wall bracket. They evaluated Tom's sign layout, signed it off pending vector print files, and confirmed costs at under four hundred pounds per sign. They also discussed counter drift, agreeing to rely on nightly resets and conduct spot checks, and evaluated the design against survey feedback, deciding against adding a QR code for a future app.
